# internal-dns: prod.internal names failing to resolve

Networking, team-platform. Read the first section even if you're in a hurry. Most wrong turns in DNS incidents come from not knowing which resolver answered.

## How a prod.internal name gets resolved

Every service finds its datastores by name: inventory-service connects to `inventory-db-01.prod.internal`, payments-api reaches payments-db through the payments-pgbouncer names, and so on. Those names live in one zone, `prod.internal`, and two servers are authoritative for it:

- internal-dns-01.prod.internal (10.0.0.53)
- internal-dns-02.prod.internal (10.0.0.54)

Both are VMs running CoreDNS (systemd unit `coredns`, config `/etc/coredns/Corefile`). Each serves the zone from a local zone file through CoreDNS's `file` plugin, which reloads the zone when its SOA serial changes. Records carry a 60 s TTL, and the SOA's negative-caching TTL is also 60 s. Each VM has its own copy of the file. The rollout tool updates them one after the other, so for a short time during a rollout the two can differ.

Clients reach the two servers by different paths:

- **VMs** list both servers in `/etc/resolv.conf`, internal-dns-01 first. glibc asks nameservers in the order listed. It moves to the second when the first doesn't answer, or when it answers over UDP with SERVFAIL, REFUSED or NOTIMP. An NXDOMAIN from the first server is a final answer, and glibc doesn't ask the second. So VMs follow internal-dns-01's answers unless it is down or failing. That holds only while the order stays as it is and `options rotate` isn't set.
- **Pods** ask the cluster's own CoreDNS. Its Corefile has a server block for `prod.internal` with `cache 30` and `forward . 10.0.0.53 10.0.0.54`. The `forward` plugin picks an upstream at random for each query it sends. The cache holds each answer, positive or negative, for at most 30 s, and every refresh can land on either server. If the two servers disagree, pods see whichever answer was cached last, and that changes from one cache period to the next.

## What the two codes mean here

**NXDOMAIN**: the server that answered says the name doesn't exist in the zone. This is an answer, not a failure, so CoreDNS's `forward` plugin keeps treating that server as healthy, and Go's resolver doesn't try another server after an NXDOMAIN. Go reports it as `no such host`.

**SERVFAIL**: the server couldn't produce an answer at all. For a `prod.internal` name that usually means the zone isn't loaded on that server, or CoreDNS there is unhealthy. Go reports it as `server misbehaving`.

They need different fixes. NXDOMAIN almost always means the zone content is wrong. SERVFAIL means the server is wrong.

## Investigation

### Separate real failures from search-domain noise

A pod's `/etc/resolv.conf` uses `ndots:5` and search domains `<namespace>.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local`. A name like `inventory-db-01.prod.internal` has only two dots, so the resolver first tries it with each search suffix, and each of those attempts gets NXDOMAIN from the cluster zone before the real name is asked. Cluster DNS always shows lots of NXDOMAIN. That is normal and tells you nothing. Only count NXDOMAIN for the `prod.internal` zone (the cluster CoreDNS metrics can be split by zone), or grep application logs for the exact name that failed.

### Find the exact name and who is affected

From the application side, search for `no such host` or `server misbehaving` with the hostname:

```
kubectl -n commerce logs deploy/inventory-service --since=30m \
  | grep -oE 'lookup [^ ]+ on [^ ]+: (no such host|server misbehaving)' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
```

Note whether the failures are constant or come and go, and whether VM-based services (the datastores, the bouncers) have the same problem. Pods failing intermittently while VMs are fine is the fingerprint of the two servers disagreeing.

### Ask each server directly

From any VM, bypassing every cache:

```
dig @10.0.0.53 inventory-db-01.prod.internal +norecurse
dig @10.0.0.54 inventory-db-01.prod.internal +norecurse
dig @10.0.0.53 prod.internal SOA +short
dig @10.0.0.54 prod.internal SOA +short
```

Read the `status:` in each header and compare the SOA serials.

- Same serial and the same answer from both: the zone is consistent. If the answer is NXDOMAIN on both, the record really is missing. Check the most recent zone change.
- Different serials, and only one server returns NXDOMAIN: a partial rollout. The server with the newer serial has the content that broke.
- SERVFAIL from one server: look at that server's logs.

```
ssh internal-dns-02.prod.internal 'sudo journalctl -u coredns --since "-1h" | tail -50'
ssh internal-dns-02.prod.internal 'sudo systemctl status coredns --no-pager'
```

### Check the zone file itself

On each VM, compare the file you expect with the one on disk:

```
ssh internal-dns-01.prod.internal 'grep -n "inventory-db-01" /etc/coredns/zones/prod.internal.db'
ssh internal-dns-02.prod.internal 'grep -n "inventory-db-01" /etc/coredns/zones/prod.internal.db'
```

## Fixing it

**Record missing on one or both servers.** Restore the record in the zone source, bump the SOA serial, and roll the file to *both* servers. Confirm with the `dig` commands that both return the record with the same serial. A file with an unchanged serial isn't reloaded, so the bump is not optional.

**Rollout stuck halfway.** Either finish it (if the new content is right) or roll the old file back to the server that got it, again with a higher serial than either server has now.

**SERVFAIL from one server.** Restart CoreDNS there (`sudo systemctl restart coredns`) and recheck. If it fails to start, read the journal before doing anything else: a broken Corefile or zone file is the usual reason. While one server is broken, VMs move to the other when it times out or answers SERVFAIL or REFUSED. Pods will still send some queries to the broken one.

**Pods still failing after both servers agree.** Wait out the cluster cache. Negative answers are held for at most 30 s under the `cache 30` cap. If you can't wait, restart the cluster DNS: `kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deploy/coredns`.

## Verification

- Both servers return the record with the same SOA serial.
- `no such host` for the name is gone from the application logs for 15 minutes.
- Cluster DNS NXDOMAIN for the `prod.internal` zone is back at its baseline.

## Background: the March 2026 incident

A zone-file rollout reached internal-dns-02 only (serial bumped, zone reloaded) and the new file was missing `inventory-db-01.prod.internal`. internal-dns-01 still had the old file. inventory-service-01 and inventory-service-02 logged `no such host` intermittently: each cluster DNS cache period got its answer from whichever server `forward` picked. The datastore VMs weren't affected because their resolv.conf lists internal-dns-01 first. Comparing the two SOA serials found it in minutes. The fix was to restore the record and roll the corrected file to both servers.
title: internal-dns: SERVFAIL or NXDOMAIN for prod.internal names

# Five-second checkouts: one lookup, eight questions

My notes from the third evening of the June 2026 checkout slowdown, tidied up. I've left the dead ends in, because that's where the time went.

## What you need to know first

orders-api is Node on a Debian-based image, so name resolution goes through glibc. Node's `dns.lookup`, which `pg` and the HTTP client use underneath, doesn't resolve anything on the event loop. It hands `getaddrinfo` to libuv's worker pool, which has 4 threads unless `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` says otherwise. The same 4 threads serve file system calls and some crypto. While a lookup hangs, it keeps one of them busy.

Our `pg` Pool (`max` 25 per pod) had `idleTimeoutMillis` at its default, 10 seconds. Checkout traffic arrives in bursts, so the pool closed idle connections between bursts and opened fresh ones at the start of the next. Every fresh connection begins with a lookup of `orders-db-01.prod.internal`.

## The notes

**17 June, 20:40.** Paged: `/checkout` p99 above 5 s, third evening in a row. p50 normal. It comes in bursts of a minute or two, then goes quiet.

**20:55.** Edge access logs for `/checkout`: status `200`, no response flag, `x-envoy-upstream-service-time` about equal to the total. The time is spent inside orders-api. The slow requests aren't spread out: they bunch just above 5 s, with a smaller group just above 10 s.

**21:10.** Not the heap. Memory per pod flat, no restarts, GC pause time normal, event-loop lag low. Whatever waits isn't holding the loop.

**21:15.** Durations stacked at multiples of five seconds smell like a timeout being hit and retried, not like slow work. The resolver's default timeout is 5 s. Time the lookups themselves.

**21:25.** Timed 200 lookups from inside a pod, through the same call the app makes:

```
kubectl -n commerce exec deploy/orders-api -- node -e '
const dns = require("dns"); let n = 0;
(function next() {
  const t = Date.now();
  dns.lookup("orders-db-01.prod.internal", () => {
    console.log(Date.now() - t);
    if (++n < 200) next();
  });
})();' | sort -n | tail -5
```

Most took 1 to 3 ms. Two took just over 5,000 ms. So: lookups, not queries.

**21:40.** Why would a lookup ever wait, with cluster DNS looking healthy on every dashboard? The pod's resolver config:

```
$ kubectl -n commerce exec deploy/orders-api -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
search commerce.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
nameserver <cluster DNS service IP>
options ndots:5
```

`ndots:5` means a name with fewer than five dots gets each search suffix appended first, and is asked as written only after those. Our database name has two dots. So one lookup is four names: three suffixed ones, each answered with NXDOMAIN (quickly), then the real one. glibc asks for an A and an AAAA record per name. **One lookup is 4 names × 2 record types = 8 queries over UDP.**

UDP doesn't promise delivery, and now and then a reply is lost. We never found out why on this cluster. When a reply is missing, the resolver waits out its 5 s timeout and asks that query again; the retry usually succeeds, so the lookup just comes back 5 s late. Two lost replies on two different queries of the same lookup, each recovered by its retry, cost about 10 s: still a `200`, just slow. That's the 10 s group. `getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN` needs both tries of one query lost (the default is `attempts:2`), which is rarer still; a handful of those lines from those evenings were in the logs, for a name that resolved fine whenever I tried it.

Eight chances per lookup to lose a reply, not two. That's what lifted a rare event into the p99.

**21:50.** Why did whole bursts suffer, not only the requests that opened a connection? Four libuv threads. A burst opened a dozen connections at once; with two or three of those lookups sitting in a 5 s wait, every other lookup and file read queued for the remaining threads.

## What changed on 18 June

1. `dnsConfig` on the orders-api Deployment:

   ```yaml
   dnsConfig:
     options:
       - name: ndots
         value: "2"
   ```

   With `ndots:2`, a two-dot name is asked as written first, so `orders-db-01.prod.internal` resolves in 2 queries instead of 8: a quarter of the exposure. Names with no dot or one dot still walk the search list, so calls to other in-cluster services behave as before.

2. `idleTimeoutMillis: 60000` on the `pg` Pool, so a quiet minute between bursts doesn't throw connections away.

We didn't raise `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`. More threads would have hidden the stalls without making any lookup faster.

## Signs it's this again

- Slow requests stack near 5 s or 10 s; the edge says the time is inside the service.
- Heap and event loop healthy.
- A timed `dns.lookup` loop from a pod shows rare outliers around 5,000 ms.
- `getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN` for a name that resolves when you try it by hand.
- The name has fewer dots than the pod's `ndots`.

No 5 s outliers on `/checkout` since 18 June. orders-api is the only Deployment that sets its own `ndots`; everything else keeps the cluster default of 5.
title: orders-api: slow name lookups from search-domain expansion

# Cluster DNS is falling over

Pods never talk to internal-dns themselves. Each pod's resolver points at the cluster DNS Service: the `coredns` Deployment in `kube-system`, pods labelled `k8s-app=kube-dns`, 4 replicas. It answers cluster names on its own and forwards `prod.internal` to the two internal-dns VMs. When it's overloaded, everything in every namespace that needs a name suffers in the same minute.

## Is it this?

- [ ] Errors from several services in different namespaces, all starting together. Each runtime words it its own way:
  - Go (auth-service, payments-api, inventory-service): `lookup <name> on <cluster DNS IP>:53: ... i/o timeout`
  - Node (orders-api, notification-worker): `getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN <name>`
  - Python (catalog-api, fraud-scorer): `[Errno -3] Temporary failure in name resolution`
- [ ] Names of every kind fail: `auth-db-01.prod.internal`, `catalog-db-01.prod.internal`, and short in-cluster Service names as well. One bad record would never touch cluster names.
- [ ] Requests on connections that were already open keep working. Failures land on new connections, so whichever service reconnects most shows it first.
- [ ] The datastore VMs don't notice anything: they ask internal-dns directly.

## Rule out internal-dns

- [ ] From any VM, ask both servers and read the status and timing:

  ```
  for s in 10.0.0.53 10.0.0.54; do dig @$s auth-db-01.prod.internal | grep -E 'status:|Query time'; done
  ```

  `NOERROR` in a few milliseconds from both means the authoritative side is fine. Don't touch it.

## Look at the cluster DNS pods

- [ ] `kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o wide`: all Running and Ready? Restarts?
- [ ] `kubectl -n kube-system top pod -l k8s-app=kube-dns`: each pod near its CPU limit is the usual picture.
- [ ] Grafana, CoreDNS dashboard: requests per pod, the p99 of `coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds`, and `coredns_cache_hits_total` against `coredns_cache_misses_total`. Overload looks like p99 jumping from milliseconds to seconds while the request rate sits at or above its usual peak.
- [ ] One replica's log: `kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/coredns --since=15m | tail -50`. Upstream errors naming 10.0.0.53 or 10.0.0.54 point back at internal-dns. None, and the pods are simply busy.

## Relieve it

- [ ] Add replicas: `kubectl -n kube-system scale deploy/coredns --replicas=<n>`. Doubling the replicas halves each one's share. New pods take queries once Ready, usually inside a minute.
- [ ] Pods pinned at their CPU limit and no room for more of them: raise the limit, leave the request.
- [ ] Don't restart the Deployment as a fix. Restarting overloaded pods removes capacity while they come back.
- [ ] Errors should fade within a couple of minutes of the new replicas being Ready. Apps retry lookups on their next request; nothing on the app side needs a restart.

## Afterwards

- [ ] Record the peak query rate and how many replicas it took. The replica count is fixed by hand, not autoscaled.
- [ ] Write a manual scale-up back into the Deployment's source, or the next rollout quietly undoes it.

## History

February 2025: the cluster had grown, the replica count hadn't. At the evening peak, about 19:50, both replicas sat at their CPU limit and lookups began timing out in auth-service, catalog-api and orders-api together. internal-dns answered at once when asked directly. The page came at 19:56. Scaling `coredns` from 2 to 4 replicas at 20:08 cleared it by 20:15, and it has run with 4 since.
title: Cluster DNS overloaded: lookups timing out in every namespace

```
   2071 [pod/card-processor-proxy-7d9f…-a]

subject=CN = <our merchant id>

notAfter=Jan 14 00:00:00 2025 GMT

$ openssl req -new -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout client.key -out client.csr -subj "/CN=<our merchant id>"

# 5. check what came back before loading it
$ openssl x509 -in client.crt -noout -issuer -enddate
$ diff <(openssl x509 -in client.crt -noout -pubkey) <(openssl pkey -in client.key -pubout) && echo key matches

# 6. replace the Secret, then restart: the proxy only reads it at start.
#    The Deployment rolls one instance at a time (maxSurge 0, maxUnavailable 1), so while it rolls
#    one proxy carries everything and the egress budget is halved (180 instead of 360 per second).
#    Off-peak, or expect CPX-W430 for the minute or two it takes.
$ k create secret tls card-processor-client-tls --cert=client.crt --key=client.key --dry-run=client -o yaml | k apply -f -
$ k rollout restart deploy/card-processor-proxy && k rollout status deploy/card-processor-proxy

$ k logs -l app=card-processor-proxy --prefix --tail=-1 --since=2m | grep -c CPX-E600
0
```

# auth-db server certificate: questions and answers

Scope: auth-db-01.prod.internal (primary) and auth-db-02.prod.internal (replica), PostgreSQL 16 on VMs. Maintainer: team-dba.

**What is the arrangement?**

auth-service connects as `auth_app` with `sslmode=verify-full`. It checks that the server certificate chains to our internal CA, that it is within its validity dates, and that its name matches the host it dialled. The server's certificate and key are `server.crt` and `server.key` in `/etc/postgresql/16/main/`. A systemd timer, `pg-cert-renew.timer`, requests a new certificate from the internal CA 30 days before expiry and writes it over the old files.

**How does an expired certificate show up?**

auth-service logs connection errors containing `tls error` and `x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid`, and logins fail with `503`. On the database side nothing looks wrong. Postgres raises no warning about its own certificate, and the connection count is normal or lower than usual.

**Why doesn't everything fail at the same moment?**

The certificate is checked when a connection is opened, never again afterwards. auth-service's pgx pool (`pool_max_conns=30` per pod) keeps connections for up to `pool_max_conn_lifetime=1h` and closes those idle longer than `pool_max_conn_idle_time=30m`; both are set in its `DATABASE_URL`. After expiry, connections that were already open carry on working, and every new one fails. Over the following hour the older connections age out, the pool can't replace them, and the failures climb. Errors that keep growing for tens of minutes, while the database looks healthy, are the signature.

**The file on disk is valid. Why is the server presenting an expired certificate?**

Postgres reads `ssl_cert_file` and `ssl_key_file` when it starts and when its configuration is reloaded. Writing new files changes nothing until one of those happens. Compare what the server sends with what is on disk:

```
openssl s_client -starttls postgres -connect auth-db-01.prod.internal:5432 </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -serial -enddate
sudo openssl x509 -in /etc/postgresql/16/main/server.crt -noout -serial -enddate
```

Different serials mean the server is still on the old certificate.

**How do we make it pick up the new one?**

Reload, don't restart:

```sql
SELECT pg_reload_conf();
```

`sudo systemctl reload postgresql@16-main` does the same. New connections get the new certificate, and existing sessions carry on undisturbed. A restart would also work, but it drops every session for no gain.

**Does the replica need the same?**

Yes. auth-db-02 has its own certificate and its own timer. Check and reload it the same way, even if nothing connects to it at the moment.

**What if the timer never got a new certificate at all?**

Then the files on disk are old too. `systemctl list-timers pg-cert-renew.timer` and `journalctl -u pg-cert-renew.service --since "-31d"` show the last runs and their errors. Ask the internal CA's owners for a certificate by hand, install both files owned by `postgres` with mode `0600` on the key, and reload.

**Can auth-service just stop verifying for now?**

No. `sslmode=require` keeps the encryption but accepts any certificate, including one from whoever sits in the path. That changes auth-service's security posture; it is not an incident fix.

**Has this happened?**

On 2025-04-08 the certificate on auth-db-01 expired at 09:00 UTC. The timer had written a valid replacement on 2025-03-09, but nothing told Postgres to load it. New connections from auth-service began failing at 09:00 while the older ones aged out over the next hour, and the error-rate alert paged at 09:38. At 09:47 `s_client` showed the old serial. `pg_reload_conf()` at 09:51 fixed it, and logins were normal again by 09:53. auth-db-02 was reloaded too.

Since 2025-04-09 the timer reloads Postgres after it writes the files.
title: auth-db: expired server certificate still being served

# Reference card: the edge's public certificate

## What it is

The certificate edge-gateway presents on port 443 to every client. A public CA issues it. It is stored in the Secret `edge-public-tls` (namespace `platform`) and mounted into each edge pod as files. Envoy reads those files when it starts, so a renewed Secret takes effect only after `kubectl -n platform rollout restart deploy/edge-gateway`.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Validated by | Clients: browsers, mobile apps, partner integrations |
| Loaded on | edge-gateway-01, -02 and -03, each pod on its own |
| Restart behaviour | 3 pods; surge 1, unavailable 0: one new pod at a time, three serving throughout |
| Renewal | team-platform, 30 days before expiry |
| Watch | an outside probe checks the expiry date daily |

## What an expired certificate looks like from inside

Clients abandon the handshake before sending any HTTP. Envoy never sees a request, so:

- nothing in the access log, so no response flag and no 5xx
- request rates fall across all routes at the same moment
- successful handshakes (`listener.<address>.ssl.handshake`) drop off with them
- `listener.<address>.ssl.connection_error` (TLS errors other than failed certificate verification) is worth watching, but Envoy's docs don't say whether a client rejecting our certificate is counted there

Envoy's admin listener (9901) is reachable only inside each pod. Forward it from one pod at a time:

```
kubectl port-forward -n platform <edge-gateway pod name> 9901
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9901/stats | grep -E 'ssl\.(handshake|connection_error)'
```

## What clients actually receive

```
openssl s_client -connect edge-gateway-02.prod.internal:443 -servername <public hostname> </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -enddate
```

Run it against all three pods. A pod that missed its restart keeps serving the old certificate. Always pass `-servername`: without SNI, Envoy may answer from a different filter chain.

## Four failures that all look like "the certificate"

| Problem | `openssl s_client` (verify result) | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Leaf expired | `Verify return code: 10 (certificate has expired)`; leaf `notAfter` in the past | Renew, update the Secret, restart |
| Intermediate missing from the file | `Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)` | Put leaf then intermediate in the certificate file |
| Intermediate expired | Code 10, but `-showcerts` shows the expired date on the intermediate | Fetch the CA's current chain |
| Client clock wrong | One client fails, everyone else fine | Client side; nothing to change at the edge |

## Done when

All three pods serve the new `notAfter`, request rates are back to their usual shape for an hour, and `ssl.handshake` climbs at its normal pace.
title: edge-gateway public TLS certificate: reference

# Did today's release do this?

For when auth-service misbehaves and something shipped today. Namespace `identity`, Deployment `auth-service`, 2 pods (auth-service-01.prod.internal and -02 in logs). Our rollouts keep the Deployment defaults: with 2 replicas that's one extra pod at a time and none removed early, so for a few minutes old and new versions serve side by side.

**Q1. Did the trouble begin during or soon after a rollout?**

```
kubectl -n identity rollout history deploy/auth-service
kubectl -n identity get rs -l app=auth-service -o wide
```

The newest ReplicaSet's AGE is when the rollout began.

- No rollout in the last few hours → not a deploy problem. Leave this page.
- Yes → Q2.

**Q2. Do the errors follow the new pods?**

```
kubectl -n identity get pods -l app=auth-service -L pod-template-hash
for p in $(kubectl -n identity get pods -l app=auth-service -o name); do
  echo "$p $(kubectl -n identity logs "$p" --since=20m | grep -c AUTH-E401X)"
done
```

- Errors sit on the new hash, or start the minute the first new pod turned Ready → the release. Go to Q3.
- Errors spread evenly over old and new pods → something they share. Check dependencies before blaming the code. For session errors: `redis-cli -h redis-sessions-02.prod.internal ROLE` shows which node is primary; an unchanged primary and no Redis write errors in auth-service's logs rule out a Redis switch.

**Q3. Did the release change anything stored or shared?**

Read the diff for: session or cache encodings, key names, database migrations, message formats, feature-flag defaults.

- Nothing of the kind → Q4.
- Yes → Q5.

**Q4. Roll back.**

```
kubectl -n identity rollout undo deploy/auth-service
kubectl -n identity rollout status deploy/auth-service
```

Errors should stop as old pods take over, about six minutes for both. Keep the bad ReplicaSet (don't delete it) so the squad can debug, and tell them.

**Q5. Data written by the new version: stop and think before rolling back.**

Every minute the new version runs, it writes things in its own format. A rollback means the old version meets those things.

- The old version can read what the new one wrote → Q4.
- It can't → both directions hurt. Staying forward breaks what the old version wrote; going back breaks what the new one wrote. Choose the smaller harm. Often the better move is a fast fix-forward that reads both formats, left running until the old data expires.
- Rolling back anyway: warn support that a second wave of errors is coming, from data written during the bad window.

**Q6. Done when** `AUTH-E401X` is back to its usual trickle on both pods for 30 minutes, and the ReplicaSet serving traffic is the one you meant.

## July 2026, for the record

A release changed how session values under the `sess:` prefix in redis-sessions were encoded. New pods couldn't decode sessions written by old pods, and the reverse. The rollout began at 14:05. At 14:08, as the first new pod became Ready, `AUTH-E401X` jumped and followed every request that reached a pod of the other version. By 14:11 both pods ran the new code, and every user holding an old-format session had been logged out once.

The page came at 14:14. Redis was checked first and was fine: same primary, no write errors. We rolled back at 14:20. From 14:23, as the first old-version pod returned, everyone who had logged in since 14:08 was logged out a second time; that wave faded by about 14:30.

No data was lost. The sessions were still in Redis; they just couldn't be read. On 2026-07-22 we shipped a version that reads both encodings. Looking back, the answer at Q5 was fix-forward.
title: Is it the release? auth-service rollouts and safe rollback

# Pushing config to VMs

Maintained by the config-management maintainers in team-platform. Covers files the rollout tool pushes to VM-hosted daemons. Application services on Kubernetes roll out through their Deployments and are out of scope here.

## How the tool behaves

It pushes to one host first, the canary, then restarts or reloads the unit. It waits 60 s, checks that the unit is active, and runs a probe for that service. Only if both pass does it move to the next host, one at a time. On the first failure it stops and leaves the remaining hosts alone.

That gate applies only to units in its probe table:

| Unit | Probe |
|---|---|
| `kafka` | `kafka-broker-api-versions.sh --bootstrap-server <host>:9092` |
| `opensearch` | `curl -s http://<host>:9200/_cluster/health` |
| `redis-server` | `redis-cli -h <host> PING` |
| `redis-sentinel` | `redis-cli -h <host> -p 26379 PING` |
| `coredns` | `dig @<host> prod.internal SOA` |
| `postgresql@16-main` | `pg_isready -h <host>` |

A unit missing from the table still gets the older pacing: canary, a fixed 5-minute wait, the next host, and no check beyond the exit status of `systemctl restart`. Enrolling a unit means adding a row; ask us.

## Before the push

1. **Validate what can be validated.** For Postgres, place the file, then before any restart run `SELECT name, setting, error FROM pg_file_settings WHERE error IS NOT NULL;`. It lists every line the server couldn't apply, with the reason. A setting that only takes effect at restart also gets a message there, so read each row rather than treating any row as fatal. The other daemons have no dry run on our hosts, so read the diff against the daemon's documented types. A size written where an integer is expected is the classic mistake.
   *Why:* a daemon that rejects its config at startup stays down, and a restart is exactly when it reads the file.
2. **Choose the canary.** Pick the least-loaded host, and never a datastore's only host. Single-instance datastores get their own run, off-peak, with someone watching.
3. **Know what one host down costs.** Kafka here has replication factor 3 and `min.insync.replicas=2`. Losing one broker costs redundancy, not writes. Losing two stops every `acks=all` producer.

## During the push

4. **Watch the canary yourself**, not only the tool:
   `ssh <host> 'systemctl is-active <unit>; sudo journalctl -u <unit> --since "-5min" | tail -20'`
   *Why:* `systemctl restart` can report success for a process that dies seconds later. Our `kafka` unit is `Type=simple`, so systemd counts it as started as soon as the process launches.
5. **If the tool stops on a failure, don't rerun it.** A rerun starts at the canary again with the same bad file.

## When a daemon won't come back

6. **Stop the run** if the tool hasn't stopped itself, which is the case for any unit outside the table.
7. **Read why it refused:** `sudo journalctl -u <unit> -n 100`. A bad Kafka value ends startup with a line like:
   `org.apache.kafka.common.config.ConfigException: Invalid value 10MB for configuration message.max.bytes: Not a number of type INT`
8. **Revert by pushing the previous commit**, not by editing on the host; hand edits vanish at the next push. Push only to the failed hosts, then start the unit (`sudo systemctl start kafka`).
9. **Confirm recovery.** Run the unit's probe, then check health at the service level. For Kafka, this should print nothing once every replica is back in sync:
   `/opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-03.prod.internal:9092 --describe --under-replicated-partitions`
10. **Fix the change**, have it reviewed again, and push it as a new run.

## Why the gate exists: 2026-08-13

A change set `message.max.bytes=10MB` in `/opt/kafka/config/server.properties`, meaning to allow 10 MB messages. Kafka expects a plain number of bytes there. At the time, the tool used the older pacing for every unit.

- **10:12** kafka-01, the canary, restarted and exited seconds later on the `ConfigException`. No alert: the under-replicated alert needs 10 minutes.
- **10:17** After the fixed wait, kafka-02 got the same file and died the same way. With one broker left, no partition could keep two in-sync replicas, so every `acks=all` write failed. Clients logged lines such as `Connection to node 1 (kafka-01.prod.internal/10.0.33.11:9092) could not be established. Node may not be available.`
- **10:19** Page on producer errors. **10:20** Run stopped; kafka-03 was due at 10:22.
- **10:25** Previous file pushed to kafka-01 and kafka-02, and both started. **10:27** Both up. **10:36** Every replica back in sync.

For those ten minutes without writes:

- ledger-service logged `LEDGER-E455` for each entry it couldn't publish, queued them, retried with backoff and had drained the queue by 10:28. Its CPU didn't move.
- Checkout didn't notice. orders-api writes order events to an outbox table in orders-db first, and the relay that publishes them fell behind, then caught up.
- notification-worker had nothing new to read, so its lag stayed flat.

The gate went live on 2026-08-20.
title: Config pushes to VMs: a daemon that doesn't come back

# Worked example: the migration that waited (15 May 2025)

A replay written by the catalog squad. The migration itself was harmless. What hurt was everything that lined up behind it.

## The setup that afternoon

- catalog-api (namespace `catalog`; catalog-api-01 and -02 in logs) serves requests with async workers. Each pod's SQLAlchemy pool allows 10 connections plus 5 overflow, so at most 30 sessions on catalog-db-01.prod.internal.
- redis-cache served about 95% of product reads. That afternoon catalog-api handled roughly 1,200 product reads a second, about 60 of which missed the cache and went to catalog-db. On top of that came about 5 writes a second (price and stock edits) to `products`.
- Schema changes ship as Alembic migrations, run by the pre-deploy Job `catalog-api-migrate`. The Deployment rolls only if the Job succeeds.
- A weekly export reads all of `products` to rebuild the search index, inside one transaction of about 40 minutes.
- **There was no `lock_timeout` on migrations then.** It dates from 2025-05-16, the day after. A migration waiting for a lock would wait as long as it took.

## Minute by minute

**13:30.** The weekly export begins. Its open transaction holds an `ACCESS SHARE` lock on `products` until it ends. Ordinary reads and writes don't conflict with that.

**14:02:00.** The release's migration runs `ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN discontinued_at timestamptz;`. Adding a nullable column with no default is quick, but it needs an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, if only for an instant, and that conflicts with the export's lock. The ALTER waits.

> *What it meant:* a lock request that conflicts with one already *waiting* queues behind it, even when it would be compatible with the lock actually held. From here on, every new `SELECT` or `UPDATE` on `products` waited behind the ALTER, which waited behind the export.

**14:02:00 to about 14:02:00.5.** Cache misses and writes reached catalog-db at about 65 a second, and each one stuck while holding its pool connection. At that rate, 30 connections were gone in under half a second.

> *What the graphs showed afterwards:* the pool graph jumped from a handful in use to 30 between two scrapes.

**14:02:15.** First `504`s at the edge, for requests stuck since 14:02:00 that reached the 15-second route timeout. Requests answered from the cache kept succeeding, so most product pages still loaded.

**14:02:30.** catalog-api started logging

```
QueuePool limit of size 10 overflow 5 reached, connection timed out, timeout 30.00
```

for requests that had waited 30 seconds for a connection. The edge had already given up on those at 15 seconds, so clients only ever saw `504`.

**14:06.** The edge alert on the `504` rate paged the catalog on-call.

> *What it meant:* about 5% of product reads and every product write were failing while catalog-db looked idle.

**14:07.** catalog-db-01: CPU low, no `CAT-E301` from catalog-api, 32 sessions in use out of 97 usable. Not load, not slots.

**14:08.** Who waits on whom:

```sql
SELECT pid, usename, wait_event_type, wait_event,
       pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by,
       now() - query_start AS waiting,
       left(query, 60) AS stmt
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = current_database() AND state <> 'idle'
ORDER BY xact_start;
```

First row: the export, active. Second: the ALTER, `wait_event_type = Lock`, `wait_event = relation`, blocked by the export's pid. Then 30 `catalog_app` sessions, each blocked by the ALTER's pid.

**14:09.** Cancelled the migration, not the export:

```sql
SELECT pg_cancel_backend(<pid of the ALTER>);
```

The queue emptied at once, connections came back, and the `504`s stopped within the minute. The Job failed, so the Deployment never rolled and the new code wasn't serving yet.

> *Why the ALTER and not the export:* cancelling the export also clears the queue, but it throws away 40 minutes of work, and the ALTER had to be retried anyway.

**14:10.** The export finished by itself.

**14:40.** Migration rerun with a lock timeout. The column was added in milliseconds.

## What changed

Since 2025-05-16 the migration Job runs with `PGOPTIONS='-c lock_timeout=5s'`. A migration that can't get its lock within 5 seconds fails instead of building a queue, and the Job retries it a few times after a pause. Five seconds of queued requests is a blip; seven minutes was an incident.

Before a release that includes a migration, the squad now also checks for long transactions on the target table, and doesn't release during the weekly export.

## What the on-call does in one

1. Find the waiting DDL (`wait_event_type = 'Lock'`, a statement starting `ALTER`, `DROP`, or `CREATE INDEX` without `CONCURRENTLY`) and what blocks it.
2. Cancel the DDL with `pg_cancel_backend`. The queue clears immediately.
3. Confirm the deploy didn't carry on without its migration.
4. Rerun the migration with `lock_timeout` once the long transaction has finished.
title: catalog-api: a migration's lock queue stalls cache-miss reads and writes on products

# card-processor-proxy egress limiter

Reference card, team-payments.

## Terms

**Processor limit.** The card processor accepts at most 400 requests per second for our merchant account, all our traffic combined. Above that it answers 429, and the proxy logs `CPX-W429`.

**Local limiter.** Since 2026-07-09 the proxy also limits itself, so we stay under 400 without waiting for the processor to push back. Each proxy instance has its own token bucket. Settings live in ConfigMap `card-processor-proxy-config`:

- `CPX_LOCAL_RPS=180`: tokens per second, per instance
- `CPX_LOCAL_MAX_WAIT=2s`: the longest an attempt may queue for a token

**Queueing.** An attempt that finds no token joins a queue for up to 2 s. If a token frees up in time, it goes ahead late. If not, it is rejected when the 2 s run out. A rejected attempt logs `CPX-W430` and never reaches the processor.

**What takes a token.** Every attempt payments-api makes, retries included (`CPX_MAX_ATTEMPTS=3`).

**Budget.** 2 instances × 180 = 360 per second, 90% of 400. The split is fixed: an instance doesn't know when the other has gone.

## Placement

Proxy pods run only on the `egress` node pool: 2 nodes whose outbound addresses are on the processor's allowlist, selected by a nodeSelector and a taint toleration. Required anti-affinity puts one proxy per node. If one egress node is cordoned or down, the other already holds a proxy, so the replacement stays `Pending` until the node returns. Meanwhile one instance carries everything on a budget of 180.

## Reading the signals

| Seen | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `CPX-W430` only from card-processor-proxy-01.prod.internal, -02 silent | One instance gone; the survivor's 180 is the whole budget |
| `CPX-W430` from both | Genuine traffic above 360 |
| `CPX-W429` | The processor itself pushed back |
| `PAYAPI-E1107` | A payment used all 3 attempts |

`kubectl -n payments get pods -l app=card-processor-proxy -o wide` shows where each pod runs. The missing one is `Pending`, with a scheduling event naming anti-affinity or taints.

## Arithmetic for one instance

Take a steady-state arrival rate of 240 payment requests per second at payments-api, as measured. The extra load orders-api's own retries would add once payments start failing is ignored here.

Let *r* be the share of attempts rejected. A payment fails only if all three attempts are rejected, and every admitted attempt is one successful payment. So successes = 240 × (1 − *r*³) = 180, which gives *r*³ = 0.25 and *r* ≈ 0.63.

- **Attempts reaching the limiter:** 240 × (1 + 0.63 + 0.40) ≈ 487 per second, about twice the arrivals.
- **Failed payments:** 240 × 0.25 = 60 per second of `PAYAPI-E1107`, exactly the excess over budget.
- **Time:** waiting changes delay, not these counts. Under sustained overload the queue stays full, so admitted attempts have waited close to 2 s, and rejected ones the full 2 s. A failed payment spends about 6 s in the proxy across its three attempts.

The processor sees 180 per second throughout, far under 400, and answers normally.

## Levers

1. **Bring the missing instance back.** Usually fastest: find out why its node is unschedulable and fix that.
2. **One instance for a long time.** Raise `CPX_LOCAL_RPS` to 360 on the survivor, only while it runs alone, and set it back before the second starts; two at 360 could send 720, 1.8 × the processor's limit. The change needs a proxy restart. The Deployment uses maxSurge 0 and maxUnavailable 1, and the Pending replacement already uses up that one unavailable slot, so a rollout won't take the running pod down; it has to be deleted by hand, and the new one can only start on the same node after it's gone: a gap with no proxy at all.
3. **Not a lever:** more replicas. Anti-affinity allows one per egress node.

A shared budget across instances is proposed, not built.

## Recorded case, 2026-09-16

At 19:38 the egress node under proxy-02 was cordoned and drained for a kernel patch. At 19:40 proxy-02 was evicted, and its replacement went `Pending`. Payment requests were arriving at about 240 a second. From 19:41 proxy-01 logged `CPX-W430` and payments-api logged `PAYAPI-E1107`.

The page came at 19:48. At 19:55 the logs showed proxy-01 alone, no `CPX-W429`, and normal processor latency. Raising the limit would have cost a gap with no proxy, so we waited for the patch instead. The node could only be uncordoned after the patch and its reboot finished, which was at 20:18. Uncordoned at 20:20; proxy-02 Running at 20:22; `CPX-W430` stopped at 20:23.
title: card-processor-proxy egress limiter: reference

I work on the growth team. We run the marketing emails; notification-worker does the sending. This is about the morning in March 2026 when our spring campaign sent people to search and roughly three in ten of them got an error page. Nothing was broken. A limit did exactly what it was built to do, at a size nobody had looked at in a long time.

First, how search traffic gets in. Every request passes through edge-gateway, three Envoy pods that appear in the logs as edge-gateway-01, -02 and -03. On the `/search` route, and only that route, each pod runs a local rate limiter: a bucket of tokens that refills by a fixed amount every second. A request that finds the bucket empty is turned away on the spot with status `429`, before search-api ever hears about it. Our edge marks those rejections in the response body, which carries the code `EDGE-RL01`.

Two things about that limiter caught us out. The number is per pod. In March it was 100 tokens a second on each of the three, so the whole edge let through about 300 searches a second, and only if traffic spread evenly. And the limit went in when the route was first set up, as a guard against crawlers, sized for the traffic of that time. Search traffic had grown since. The limit hadn't.

On 2026-03-10 the campaign started sending at 09:00. The first `429`s showed up at 09:05, and by 09:10 `/search` had peaked at about 420 requests a second. With 300 allowed, about 120 a second were refused, around 29%, or roughly 40 a second on each pod. team-catalog was paged at 09:12 and pulled us in once it was clear the traffic came from our send.

The first twenty minutes were confusing because every search system looked healthy. search-api had no errors, and its request rate sat flat at about 300 a second: the 420 arriving, minus the 120 the edge refused. search-cluster had plenty of headroom, with no rejections in its search thread pools, and nobody saw `SRCH-E502`. As far as search-api could tell nothing was wrong, because the refused requests never reached it. The problem was visible in one place only, the edge.

Once someone filtered the edge access logs to `/search`, it was obvious: a wall of `429`s, every body carrying `EDGE-RL01`. The limiter keeps its own counters too, which you can read on each edge pod through Envoy's admin port:

```
kubectl -n platform port-forward pod/<edge pod> 9901:9901
curl -s localhost:9901/stats | grep http_local_rate_limit
```

The `enforced` counter (requests that actually got the `429`) was rising on all three pods at about the same pace. If it had risen on one pod only, traffic would have been landing unevenly, and a bigger limit wouldn't have been the right fix.

team-catalog checked that search-cluster could absorb the extra load (it could, at around 40% CPU) and raised the limit to 250 a second per pod. That's 750 for the edge, about 1.8 times the campaign's peak. The limiter's settings live in the ConfigMap `edge-gateway-envoy`, and Envoy reads them only at startup, so the change meant a rolling restart of edge-gateway. It merged at 09:42, rolled out from 09:46, and the `429`s stopped at 09:50: forty-five minutes in all.

What I'd like other teams to take from this, especially people who aren't SREs:

A `429` can mean someone's limit, not a broken service. If users get `429` on search while search-api is calm, look at the edge first.

Per-pod limits add up. Change the number of edge pods, or how evenly traffic spreads across them, and the real limit changes with it.

Every limit needs an owner and a date to look at it again. This one had neither, so nobody remembered it existed until our users hit it.

And for us: big sends now come with a heads-up. Before a campaign we expect to bring a crowd, we tell team-catalog the send time and our best guess at the traffic, so they can check the limit and the cluster before we press send.

None of the other edge routes, checkout and payments included, has a local limit like this one.
title: When our campaign hit the search rate limit
